qa.title: Frequently Asked Questions
qa.subtitle: We have compiled frequently asked questions from customers about AMACHIHOSHISORA.
qa.subtitleNote: If you have questions not resolved here, please feel free to contact us.

questions.question: What are the characteristics of AMACHIHOSHISORA?
questions.answer: AMACHIHOSHISORA is a junmai daiginjo made with 100% Yamada-nishiki rice and underground water from Mount Fuji. Brewed by a brewery with 300 years of history, it combines traditional brewing techniques with the natural blessings of Fuji. Created as a true sake made only from rice and water, it embodies our determination to challenge the world.

questions.question: What is the difference between the 720ml, 500ml, and 180ml?
questions.answer: The 720ml and 500ml are the same AMACHIHOSHISORA Junmai Daiginjo, made with underground water from Mount Fuji and 100% Yamada-nishiki rice. Only the volume differs: we recommend the 720ml as a gift or for enjoying over several sittings, and the 500ml for a first purchase or a small group. The 180ml Fuji no Shizuku is a separate product, a Junmai Ginjo (55% rice polishing ratio) from the same brewery. At 180ml (one gō, the traditional Japanese serving size), it suits anyone who wants to try the taste first or finish a bottle in a single evening.

questions.question: Please tell me about the rice you use
questions.answer: AMACHIHOSHISORA uses 100% Yamada-nishiki, the finest sake brewing rice. Yamada-nishiki is known for its large grains and large shinpaku (white core), making it ideal for brewing elegant sake with little off-flavor, and is an important element supporting the quality of junmai daiginjo.

questions.question: What is underground water from Fuji?
questions.answer: It is clear groundwater that has been filtered through volcanic rock layers over many years after rain and snow that fell on Mount Fuji penetrated underground. It is soft water with good mineral balance, ideal for sake brewing, and forms the foundation of AMACHIHOSHISORA's taste.

questions.question: How is delivery handled?
questions.answer: We deliver under appropriate temperature control to maintain product quality. You can also specify delivery date and time.

questions.question: Please tell me the recommended way to drink
questions.answer: We recommend drinking it chilled (about 10-15°C). You can enjoy the delicate aroma and taste of junmai daiginjo to the fullest.

questions.question: Please tell me about storage methods
questions.answer: Please store in a cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, store in the refrigerator and drink as soon as possible. With proper storage, you can enjoy the original taste of AMACHIHOSHISORA for a long time.

questions.question: What is the alcohol content?
questions.answer: AMACHIHOSHISORA has an alcohol content of 15%. This is a standard level for junmai daiginjo, and you can enjoy a solid taste while having a refreshing drinking experience.

details.metaTitle: About Amachi Hoshisora & Fuji no Shizuku
details.metaDescription: Two junmai sakes brewed by Fujinishiki Brewery with Mt. Fuji underground water: Amachi Hoshisora Junmai Daiginjo and Fuji no Shizuku Junmai Ginjo. Taste, specs and how they differ.
details.title: Amachi Hoshisora & Fuji no Shizuku
details.lead: Two junmai sakes brewed with Mt. Fuji underground water by Fujinishiki Brewery in Fuji City, Shizuoka. Here is what sets each one apart.

amachi.catch: A fragrant junmai daiginjo, polished to 40%
body: Brewed from 100% Yamada-nishiki rice polished down to 40% of each grain. Using only the core of the rice keeps the flavour clean, with an elegant, fragrant aroma and a smooth mouthfeel.
It was born from the brewery's wish to take on the world with true sake made only from rice and water. A fine choice as a gift or for a special occasion.

shizuku.catch: A clear, gentle junmai ginjo in a single-serve bottle
body: Brewed from rice polished to 55%, this junmai ginjo has a clear ginjo aroma and a soft, gentle mouthfeel.
At 180ml (one gō, the traditional Japanese serving size), it suits anyone trying sake for the first time or who wants to finish a bottle in a single evening.

polish.title: Junmai Ginjo vs Junmai Daiginjo
polish.body: Both are junmai sake: brewed only from rice, rice koji and water, with no added distilled alcohol. The difference is how far the rice is polished. The polishing ratio is the share of each grain left after milling. Sake polished to 60% or less can be called ginjo, and 50% or less, daiginjo.
polish.chartLabel: Rice polishing ratio (share of each grain remaining)
polish.note: The outer layers of the grain hold more protein and fat, which can add rough flavours. The further the rice is polished, the lighter and more fragrant the sake tends to be.

brewery.title: The Brewery: Fujinishiki
body: Fujinishiki Brewery was founded in the Genroku era (1688–1704) of the Edo period in Fuji City, Shizuoka, and has been brewing at the foot of Mt. Fuji for more than 300 years.

Its brewing water is Mt. Fuji underground water: rain and snow that seep into the mountain over many years and are filtered through layers of volcanic rock. Both Amachi Hoshisora and Fuji no Shizuku are brewed with this water.

heritage.metaDescription: Fujinishiki Brewery, maker of Amachi Hoshisora, was founded in the Genroku era at the foot of Mt. Fuji. How statesman Yukio Ozaki named its sake, photographs from the Meiji era, a timeline of three centuries, and the brewery today.
heritage.title: Three centuries at the foot of Mt. Fuji
heritage.lead: Fujinishiki Brewery, which makes Amachi Hoshisora, was founded in the Genroku era (1688–1704) in Yuno, a village at the foot of Mt. Fuji. It began with a landowning family who grew rice and brewed sake from it.
heritage.heroCaption: The Fujinishiki brewery, with Mt. Fuji behind it

origin.title: How Fujinishiki got its name
body: Born in 1874 as the fourth son of the Sei family, Kintaro worked as a newspaper reporter before becoming secretary to Yukio Ozaki, and was later elected to the House of Representatives. In 1911, inspired by America’s national parks, he petitioned the Imperial Diet to create a Fuji National Park.

In 1914 Kintaro invited Ozaki, by then Minister of Justice, to the family home in Yuno. Moved by Mt. Fuji glowing like brocade in the evening sun, and by Kintaro’s return home in glory as a member of parliament, Ozaki is said to have remarked, “Fuji ni nishiki nari”: brocade upon Mt. Fuji.
Until then the family’s sake had no brand name. They took his words and named it Fujinishiki.

archive.title: The brewery in the Meiji era
archive.body: Photographs from the Meiji era, kept by Fujinishiki Brewery: the main house under construction in 1887, and the front gate, with a stable below and a room for raising silkworms above. They show a family that farmed as well as brewed.

photos.caption: The front gate in the early Meiji era. The ground floor was a stable; silkworms were raised upstairs.

items.text: The first generation founds the brewery. A local landowner who farmed rice with many tenant farmers, he begins brewing with the rice paid as rent.
Kintaro is born, fourth son of the 14th generation.
The main house is built.
Kintaro is elected to the House of Representatives.
Kintaro petitions the Imperial Diet to create a Fuji National Park.
Minister of Justice Yukio Ozaki visits Yuno. His words, “Fuji ni nishiki nari”, give the sake its name: Fujinishiki.
Kintaro dies in office at the age of 47.
Mt. Fuji is designated part of the Fuji-Hakone National Park.
Post-war land reform ends the family’s work as landowners, and brewing is suspended.
After a six-year pause, the family reopens the brewery as its main business.
The 17th generation becomes head of the brewery.
The brewery is incorporated as Fujinishiki Shuzo Co., Ltd.
Ahead of the rest of Japan, it releases Fuji Tennen Jozoshu, brewed from rice alone with no added sugar or distilled alcohol.
When Japan abolishes its sake grading system, the brewery focuses on premium special-designation sake.
The first kura-biraki (brewery open day) welcomes 400 visitors.
Shinichi Sei becomes the 18th-generation head.
A hundred years after the name was given, the brewery releases Gakudo, a commemorative sake named after Ozaki’s pen name.
Fujinishiki begins exporting its sake.
The 26th kura-biraki is held.

heritage.sourceNote: Based on Fujinishiki Brewery’s company history and “Fuji ni nishiki nari”, an essay by the 18th-generation head.

craft.title: The work of the brewery

items.title: Fields
items.text: Yuno is a cold valley swept by the fuji-oroshi wind from the mountain. Its mineral-rich spring water nurtures organically grown Yamada-nishiki rice.

items.title: Water
items.text: Rain and snow on Mt. Fuji filter through lava rock for about 70 years and emerge as very soft water, with a hardness of just 32.

items.title: Hands
items.text: In 1974, ahead of the rest of Japan, the brewery released a sake brewed from rice alone, with no added sugar or distilled alcohol.

craft.quote: Brewing sake takes a great deal of work, but I want to keep doing it with single-minded honesty, without ever cutting corners.

shizuoka.title: Shizuoka, the ginjo kingdom
body: Between 1975 and 1984, Denbei Kawamura and fellow researchers at Shizuoka’s prefectural industrial research institute worked with local brewers to develop Shizuoka yeast.
Sake brewed with it is light and clean, with fruity aromas that recall melon and banana, and it is known for bringing out the flavour of food. Shizuoka came to be called the “ginjo kingdom”.

kurabiraki.title: Kura-biraki: celebrating the new sake
body: Kura-biraki, the brewery’s open day, is a yearly celebration of the new season’s sake. Fujinishiki holds it with the Yuno village association, pouring new sake brewed with Mt. Fuji spring water.

Visitors tour the brewery, taste the new sake, shop for local produce and enjoy a children’s area. The 26th kura-biraki was held in March 2026, and the brewery wants it to be a day everyone can simply enjoy.

teaser.title: A brewery since the Genroku era
